newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finland says Russia has key to European stability.
newsitem.headline: Finland says Russia has key to European stability.

text.p: Economic progress in Russia and the emergence of a democratic system that its people could identify with and trust would be crucial for future stability in Europe, the Finnish government said on Tuesday.

In a report to the national parliament titled "Finland and the Future of Europe', the government said a desirable scenario for Europe's future would be marked by cooperation instead of confrontation and predictability instead of instability.
"Stability -- economic progress and consolidation of democratic practices -- in Russia is crucial to this end," the report said.

Finland took a decisive step by joining the EU in 1995. But after fighting two bloody wars against the Soviet Union in 1939-40 and 1941-44, the country remains keenly aware that its security is fundamentally tied to stability in Russia.

In the report, Finland said its eastern neighbour, with which it shares a 1,300 km (800 miles) border, still suffered from the concentration of economic and political power in the hands of elite groups.

"The most conspicuous players on the Russian political stage are corporatively based power blocks such as the military-industrial complex and the army, the energy complex, the agriculatural complex, financial-industrial groupings and the City of Moscow," the report said.
The Russian political system -- apparently evolving towards a strong presidency and democratic procedures based on a market economy -- could run into difficulties in the future, the report said.
It did not refer to the present instability issues surrounding the health of President Boris Yeltsin, but rather took a longer view of the situation.

"Confinement of political influence to the elite is bound to increase citizen alienation and damage the legitimacy of the system," the report said, adding: "In unfavourable circumstances, this could foster instability."
"Growing income disparities, the sudden rise in mortality, crime ... and immeasurably vast environmental problems are factors which may jeopardise the current favourable trend," it said.
The greatest challenge for Russian democracy was how to make citizens feel that the institutions of society are relevant.

"Russia has virtually no experience of a modern state or a democratic society ... By and large, the Soviet State was never based on the idea that people should feel that the system was 'their own'," the Finnish government report said.
Negative aspects of the current transition in Russia towards a capitalist market economy had impaired public faith in and respect for the political system, it said.
Unless Russian leaders built credible democratic institutions, the outcome would be "value anarchy", the report concluded.
